content: Nurses, in collaboration with other healthcare professionals, are responsible for the treatment, safety, and recovery of individuals who are acutely or chronically ill or injured. They also play a critical role in maintaining the health of well individuals and managing life-threatening emergencies across various healthcare settings. Nurses often engage in medical and nursing research and perform numerous non-clinical functions essential to the delivery of healthcare services. The education, regulation, roles, and titles of nurses differ across countries, but they generally reflect increasing levels of responsibility and professional status. Nurses develop and implement care plans in partnership with patients, their families, and other healthcare professionals and paraprofessionals. They also coordinate patient care provided by other members of the healthcare team, such as physical therapists, medical practitioners, social workers, and dietitians. Nurses frequently act as patient advocates. The structure of nursing careers varies significantly worldwide. Typically, there are distinct levels of nursing practitioners, differentiated by education, responsibility, and skill. The primary distinction lies between task-based nursing and professional nursing. Globally, there is a growing trend of employing advanced practice nurses, such as clinical nurse specialists and nurse practitioners, who are qualified to diagnose health problems, prescribe medications, and administer therapies. At the highest level of nursing education are doctoral-prepared nurses, who may hold a PhD or other doctoral degrees, specializing in research, clinical nursing, or related fields. These nurses practice, teach, and conduct research in nursing. The demand for doctoral-prepared nurses has increased as the science and art of nursing have advanced. Educational requirements for nurses vary widely across the world. For example, in some parts of Eastern Europe, nurses may be high school graduates with 12 to 18 months of training, while in Chile, registered nurses must hold at least a bachelor's degree. Nursing remains a predominantly female profession, but the number of males entering the field is steadily increasing. Governments regulate the nursing profession to ensure public safety. Healthcare settings typically involve a wide range of healthcare workers who collaborate with nurses. Examples include nursing assistants, orderlies, auxiliary nurses, and healthcare assistants, who work under the supervision of registered nurses or licensed practical nurses. These workers provide basic care, take vital signs, assist with hygiene, feeding, and psychosocial care, and perform housekeeping duties. Technicians, such as certified medication aides, phlebotomy technicians, surgical technologists, and diagnostic equipment operators, also work closely with nurses. Physicians rely on nurses' skills, observations, and expertise to ensure continuity of patient care. Pharmacists ensure the safe dispensing of medications and provide expert advice on drug therapies. Allied health professionals, such as respiratory therapists, medical technologists, speech therapists, occupational therapists, and physical therapists, collaborate with nursing staff in multidisciplinary teams. In Australia, registration as a registered nurse requires at least an associate degree, which serves as the foundation for future specialization. Postgraduate diplomas offer further vocational training in specialist areas, and master's level courses are available in both research and coursework streams. Specialist courses prepare nurses for roles such as nurse practitioners. Professional doctorates are also available. Australia has a tradition of post-basic courses, now offered as postgraduate diplomas or certificates, covering areas such as midwifery, psychiatric nursing, intensive care, and coronary care. Hospital-trained nurses can upgrade their qualifications to a Bachelor of Nursing or pursue specialist courses in their clinical areas of interest. Enrolled nurses are trained in the technical and further education (TAFE) sector, with training durations ranging from 12 to 18 months, depending on the state. In some areas, enrolled nurses are permitted to administer medications, including intravenous medications, under specific regulations. The practice of nursing in Australia is governed by state and territorial nursing regulation authorities. The Australian Nursing and Midwifery Council (ANMC) facilitates a national approach to nursing and midwifery regulation. Nurses in Australia are categorized into nurse practitioners (NP), registered nurses (RN), and enrolled nurses (EN). The professional title sister is no longer commonly used, and most nurses prefer to be addressed by their first name or their professional designation, such as RN or EN. Nurse practitioners have been introduced into the Australian healthcare system, with Victoria leading the way since 2000. This development reflects the recognition of the advanced clinical expertise some nurses have achieved in areas such as wound management. In Canada, most provinces prefer registered nurses to hold at least a bachelor's degree, preferably a Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BScN). However, Quebec grants RN status to graduates from CEGEP. While many practicing nurses are college graduates, new entrants to the profession are encouraged or required to pursue university-level education. Canadian nurses are categorized into registered nurses (RN), licensed practical nurses (LPN) or licensed vocational nurses (LVN), and registered psychiatric nurses (RPN), the latter being licensed to practice only in certain provinces and territories. The nursing profession in Canada is regulated at the provincial and territorial levels, adhering to the principles of professional regulation endorsed by the International Council of Nurses. For example, the College of Nurses of Ontario regulates both RNs and RPNs, while other provinces regulate RNs and LPNs through separate bodies. In western provinces, psychiatric nurses are governed by distinct legislation. All registered nurses and nurse practitioners in Alberta must maintain clinical competence to receive an annual practice permit from the College and Association of Registered Nurses of Alberta, which also sets standards for scope of practice and provides practice support.
